Check leaf undersides for whiteflies and monitor with sticky cards. Protect healthy plants with fine-mesh covers or reflective mulch where suitable, and ask local extension for locally appropriate vector-control options.
Keep watering even and avoid plant stress. This supports plant health but does not cure TYLCV or stop whiteflies from spreading it.
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.label: Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus
prevention: Start with healthy, locally appropriate transplants and tomato varieties listed as TYLCV-resistant or tolerant; tolerance is not immunity.
Rotate with non-host crops where practical, and remove tomato volunteers and old crop residue between plantings.

Monitor whiteflies early and use locally recommended prevention. Any pesticide, if advised, must be registered for the crop and location and used exactly according to its label and local extension advice.

Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.summary: Tomato yellow leaf curl virus (TYLCV) is a serious tomato disease spread mainly by whiteflies. Infected plants may have curled, crumpled yellow young leaves, stunted or bushy growth, and flower drop. A photo-based label is only a clue, not a confirmed diagnosis: nutrient problems, heat or water stress, and other diseases can look similar.
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.one_method: There is no cure for TYLCV; get local confirmation promptly, and remove/contain affected plants only if infection is confirmed or local extension advises it.

Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.caution: A photograph cannot confirm ToMV, and other viruses, herbicide injury, or environmental problems can look similar. Seek local extension or diagnostic-lab advice soon for confirmation and site-specific action; seek help urgently if symptoms are appearing on multiple plants or spreading. No pesticide cures a virus. If any pesticide is considered for a separately identified pest, use only a locally registered product exactly according to its label and local extension advice.
immediate_steps: If mosaic-like symptoms are present, keep the plant separate and avoid touching healthy plants after it; wash hands and clean tools between plants.
Contact your local agricultural extension service or plant-diagnostic lab promptly to confirm the cause, especially if more than one plant is affected or the crop is valuable.
If ToMV is confirmed, or local extension advises removal, pull affected plants and fallen debris, bag and discard them rather than composting; clean tools and any equipment that contacted them.
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.label: Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus
prevention: Use disease-free seed and transplants, and choose tomato varieties with resistance to ToMV where available; resistance is not complete protection against all viruses.

Use good handling sanitation, avoid tobacco products around plants, and wash hands after tobacco use and before gardening. ToMV mainly spreads through contaminated hands, tools, seed, and debris—not insect vectors, so insect spraying is not a ToMV control.
Remove volunteer tomatoes and relevant infected plant debris; ask local extension whether rotation is useful for your site, since ToMV has a broad host range and rotation alone may not prevent it.

Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.summary: This label means the photo model suspects tomato mosaic virus (ToMV) on tomato; it is not a confirmed diagnosis. Leaf mottling, curling, or distortion can have other causes, and plant viruses require lab testing for confirmation. There is no cure, so focus on preventing spread.
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.one_method: There is no cure for tomato mosaic virus; wash hands and clean tools between plants, and seek lab or extension confirmation before removing plants.

Tomato___healthy.caution: A photo-based class is only a screening result, not a confirmed diagnosis; image quality, lighting, and symptoms not visible in the photo can affect it. Confirm the plant's condition by inspecting it in person, and ask a local extension office or qualified agronomist if concerning symptoms develop or the result does not match what you see. This healthy-class guidance recommends care and monitoring only, not treatment.
immediate_steps: Check leaves, stems, and fruit regularly for new spots, wilting, yellowing, or visible insects.
Water when the soil needs it, aiming water at the soil around the base rather than wetting leaves; avoid keeping the soil waterlogged.
Keep plants supported and remove leaves that touch the ground; maintain enough space for air to move through the foliage.

prevention: Use clean mulch to help keep soil moisture steadier, and keep the area around plants free of weeds and fallen debris.
Keep notes or photos during regular checks so you can notice changes early; use locally recommended tomato varieties and rotate planting locations when feasible.
